title.value: Study Club, Labor Union or Start-Up? Characterizing Teams and Collaboration in the Bug Bounty Ecosystem
Study Club, Labor Union or Start-Up? Characterizing Teams and Collaboration in the Bug Bounty Ecosystem

abstract.value: A unique bug bounty ecosystem has evolved in China. Platforms allow groups of hackers to register together to receive team-level awards. However, little is known about the prevalence and productivity of these teams, or how team members collaborate. To address this gap, we conducted a mixed-methods study. The first stage characterized teams from a top-down ecosystem perspective. We collected bug bounty rankings from 85 platforms, using fuzzy-matching to identify 2.1k unique teams and 5.9k hunters. We show that 46% of users are registered as part of a team, and hunters with teams are more than twice as productive as hunters without teams. The typical team has less than 10 members and only operates on a handful of platforms, but we also identified mega teams participating in more than 50 platforms with hundreds of team members. The second phase provided bottom-up insights into why hackers join teams and how they collaborate within teams. Our semi-structured interviews (n = 18) reveal bug hunting teams are multi-faceted-part study club, part labor union, and part start-up. Teams act like study clubs in enabling knowledge exchange and skills development, and act like labor unions in negotiating with bug bounty platforms and vendors. Hunter teams also displayed company-like aspects when earning and sharing revenue, and also creating rules that members should follow. In doing so, hunter teams help to address three of the main challenges that bug hunters face, namely skills development, negotiating with large technology companies, and income uncertainty. 539 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

A unique bug bounty ecosystem has evolved in China. Platforms allow groups of hackers to register together to receive team-level awards. However, little is known about the prevalence and productivity of these teams, or how team members collaborate. To address this gap, we conducted a mixed-methods study. The first stage characterized teams from a top-down ecosystem perspective. We collected bug bounty rankings from 85 platforms, using fuzzy-matching to identify 2.1k unique teams and 5.9k hunters. We show that 46% of users are registered as part of a team, and hunters with teams are more than twice as productive as hunters without teams. The typical team has less than 10 members and only operates on a handful of platforms, but we also identified mega teams participating in more than 50 platforms with hundreds of team members. The second phase provided bottom-up insights into why hackers join teams and how they collaborate within teams. Our semi-structured interviews ( n = 18) reveal bug hunting teams are multi-faceted-part study club, part labor union, and part start-up. Teams act like study clubs in enabling knowledge exchange and skills development, and act like labor unions in negotiating with bug bounty platforms and vendors. Hunter teams also displayed company-like aspects when earning and sharing revenue, and also creating rules that members should follow. In doing so, hunter teams help to address three of the main challenges that bug hunters face, namely skills development, negotiating with large technology companies, and income uncertainty. 1. Introduction Bug bounty programs and platforms (BBPs) create a framework by which vendors pay external security re- searchers for discovering bugs in the vendors' systems. The first program was launched in 1995 offering cash payouts for vulnerabilities in Netscape's Navigator 2.0 browser [59]. In the following decades, many other organizations started to pay bug bounties, often facilitated by third-party interme- diary platforms like HackerOne [60]. Research has shown †Deceased, 28 March, 2024. that BBPs are an efficient security investment [8], [32], [34], [50], [55], [60], which helps explain why Google paid out $10 million in bug bounties in 2023 [42]. Despite the success of BBPs, communications between vendors and hunters is challenging. Vendors complain about low quality bug submissions [25], meanwhile hunters com- plain about slow and non-transparent decisions [1]. Another problem is the lack of established development pathways, which is especially problematic for young hackers [12] and those from diverse backgrounds [10]. Put simply, solo hunters lack market power and development opportunities. However, bug hunters do not always operate as indi- viduals. Bugcrowd, a popular bug bounty platform, allows hunters to share bounties, which might foster collabora- tion [41]. Further, in China many platforms and programs encourage the formation of bug hunting teams. The potential for collaborative bug hunting has been mentioned, but not directly investigated, in prior work (see Table 1). Research has largely focused on platforms in the so-called ‘West', and the last study that measured Chinese platforms was published in 2016 [26]. This sampling bias helps to explain why collaboration has not been directly studied. Our work addresses this gap in the literature by study- ing bug hunting teams in China. We conducted a mixed- methods study integrating quantitative data from collecting 85 BBPs and conducting semi-structured interviews with 18 bug hunters. We ask: RQ1 How are teams, hunters and rewards distributed over BBPs? RQ2 What are the functions of bug hunting teams? RQ3 Why do bug hunters join and leave teams? Contributions. Our ecosystem measurements address RQ1 and show that nearly half of the users (46%) of BBPs we measured are part of teams. Team members are more than twice as productive as solo hackers on average. The vast majority of teams (87%) have less than 10 members, but a handful of mega teams have out-sized influence on the bug bounty community. On many BBPs, a small number of teams contribute the majority of reports. The largest team has over 500 members, participating in over 60 BBPs. In answering RQ2, our findings reveal that bug bounty teams perform multifaceted functions: (i) a study club to 539 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00020 help develop skills; (ii) a union to negotiate with powerful tech companies; and (iii) a start-up to make money and manage hacker conduct. The study-club aspect sees teams invest resources in running educational seminars, sharing technical documents and tools, mentoring junior members, and problem-solving via group chat. Teams function like labor unions by intervening in negotiations with BBPs, forming alliances between teams, and even boycotting ven- dors in extreme cases. Additionally, there is a trend towards teams functioning like start-ups (iii) in pursuing revenue streams from consulting and education sessions, taking 5- 10% of team rewards as a management fee, and requiring hackers to follow a code of conduct. For RQ3, we find that bug hunters are motivated to join because teams provide hackers with skills development, prestige, and more income. However, teams also suffer organizational issues related to inactivity, member churn, poor management, and conflicts between team members, which can lead to hunters leaving the team. Terminology. In this work, we use the acronym BBP to refer to both Bug Bounty Platforms who run programs on behalf of companies, as well as Bug Bounty Programs and Security Response Centers that are run by an independent vendor. We useplatform and program to distinguish between these cases. We use the term registered team to describe teams as registered on a single BBP. We useteam to describe the the real-world organization comprising all members registered on all BBPs. 2. Related Work We contribute to two bodies of literature: (i) vulnera- bility markets described in Section 2.1; and (ii) the role of collaboration in cybersecurity described in Section 2.2. 2.1. Vulnerability Markets After Netscape announced the first BBP [59], academics started to theoretically model vulnerability markets. Authors proposed not only BBPs [4], [5] but also more exotic schemes like; selling vulnerabilities via auction [3] and brokers [6], exploit derivatives inspired by contingent con- tracts from finance [7], and vulnerability permits inspired by pollution permits from climate policy [9]. Only BBPs, where the vendor pays, and exploit/vulnerability brokers, in which governments/criminals pay, have widespread adoption. Studies of vulnerability brokers are less common be- cause the world is highly secretive [45], however excep- tions exist. Charlie Miller described his experiences selling exploits via brokers, including a photo of the $50k cheque he received from a government agency [44]. Nicole Perl- roth wrote a best selling book about this ecosystem [49]. Quantitative insights can be derived from price lists quoted by 0-day exploit brokers [43], [46], [47], although it is unclear how representative these are of actual contracts. In contrast to the secretive world of exploit brokers, empirical bug bounty research has flowered in the last decade. Table 1 shows that empirical studies use two broad methodological approaches. BBP studies collect data from bug bounty platforms and programs via scraping or data sharing agreements with the BBP. User studies collect in- terview and survey responses from participants in hunter teams. Our study is the first to combine both approaches. BBP studies have measured platforms including HackerOne [27], [28], [32], [60], Bugcrowd [50], Wooyun [32], BuTian [26] and programs from large vendors like Microsoft and Google [27]. These studies ask quantitative questions related to demographics [11], productivity [27], [32], rewards [33], [60] and longevity [50]. The last study of Chinese platforms was published in 2016 and it focused on Wooyun (which closed in 2016) and BuTian [26]. This leaves a research gap regarding the Chinese bug bounty ecosystem. User studies typically focus on the challenges and mo- tivations of bug hunters. Hunters benefit via monetary re- wards and personal growth [1]. However, there is still a barrier to entry for early-career hackers [10], [12]. Multiple studies identified that communications with vendors is a challenge [1], [14]. The problem of communications was also identified when user studies worked with vendors who receive bug reports [25], [51]. 2.2. Collaboration in Cybersecurity We frame bug hunting teams as a case-study in the broader topic of cybersecurity collaboration, which is too diffuse for a comprehensive survey. We focus on collabo- ration between individuals as part of informal structures, in our case teams, rather than collaboration within or between formal organizations, such as information sharing between firms and government entities [23]. Online forums are com- monly used by software developers to share information, even though it has been shown to be inaccurate [21], [22]. Similarly, system administrators use mailing lists to commu- nicate about patch quality [20]. Turning to offensive security, hackers also use forums to gain knowledge, with a high proportion of users active on multiple hacking forums [24]. With most relevance to our paper, research has docu- mented the role of teams to win Capture the Flag (CTF), pro- gramming competitions, and bug finding. Cuevas et al. [2] run five focus groups with top CTF teams, finding that teams divide work according to their members' special knowledge and skills. Huang et al. [58] use Kaggle as a case-study to illustrate how programmers form into teams to win compe- titions, which is “beneficial for individuals in the short term and long term”. Nosco et al. [64] propose and validate an industrialized vulnerability discovery process, emphasizing the importance of hierarchical collaboration among hackers at different levels. Notably, this approach is more suitable to companies or organizations, whereas bug hunter teams have more loosely defined structures. 2.3.
